extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy, and the theory of scientific reasoning
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analysing and assessing the correctness and use of induction, deduction, syllogism, and trains of reasoning in scientific and philosophical argument. Emphasizes when to form general propositions, how minors and majors function, and how chains of inductions combine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of syllogistic form to detect inconclusiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: The syllogistic form and rules do not describe how we necessarily reason, but furnish a mode in which reasoning may always be represented and which is admirably calculated, if the reasoning is inconclusive, to bring that inconclusiveness to light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When there is any doubt about validity, throw reasoning into syllogistic form (an induction from particulars to generals followed by deduction from those generals to particulars) in order to reveal defects. In simple familiar cases we may reason directly, but the syllogistic form is indispensable for testing doubtful arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of general propositions for retention and application
rubrics_metrics.description: General propositions allow inductions to be made once and then used repeatedly: a single careful interrogation of experience may suffice and the result be registered as a general proposition committed to memory or writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use general language to compress and retain the knowledge from many particulars, so particulars can be dismissed from memory while retaining immediately available general rules. Beware, however, that generalizations originally made on insufficient evidence can become hardened into maxims and resist revision after particulars are forgotten.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate investigation into (1) forming formulæ and (2) applying them
rubrics_metrics.description: It is natural and indispensable to separate the process of investigation into two parts: obtain general formulæ for what inferences may be drawn, and later apply those formulæ to particular cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat drawing inductions as a distinct activity from applying them; the rules of syllogism function as securities for the correctness of application. For scientific accuracy, determine distinguishing marks ahead of application so later identification is mechanical and testable.

rubrics_metrics.name: The minor premise asserts resemblance and must be verified
rubrics_metrics.description: The minor premise corresponds to asserting that a new case resembles some previously known cases in certain attributes; it is an indispensable part of the argument and must be established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating an argument, check whether the asserted resemblance (minor) is true; if not obvious by sense it requires its own induction or proof. Do not assume the minor without examining the evidence by which the new case is brought within the scope of the generalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: The major premise expresses sufficiency of evidence (but is not the induction itself)
rubrics_metrics.description: The major premise is an affirmation that the instances adduced are sufficient to authorize the conclusion — an assertion of the sufficiency or warrantableness of the induction — yet recognizing that sufficiency is not itself the inductive act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between the original inductive inference and the later recognition that evidence was sufficient. The reflexive judgment that the induction was correct is a separate reviewing act, and while useful, should not be conflated with the induction itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not reduce reasoning to analytic unfolding of concepts (reject petitio principii conflation)
rubrics_metrics.description: An argument that omits the major and reasons only from the minor to the conclusion (e.g., 'Socrates is a man, therefore Socrates is mortal') mistakes analytic recognition of meaning for empirical justification; the link asserting that the general relation holds arises from experience and not merely from meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the error of treating the meaning of terms as supplying empirical claims. Evaluate whether the relation asserted in the major is an empirical generalization supported by observed instances, not an a priori entailment from concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction followed by deduction as universal type of reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Every inference about an unobserved case is to be considered as consisting of an induction (establishing a general proposition) followed by a deduction (applying that general proposition to particulars); even if not carried out explicitly, the process is susceptible of that form and must be treated so when assurance is needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For rigorous evaluation, re-express inferences as induction + deduction to make the grounds and applications explicit. This clarifies where error may lie — in the inductive generalization, in the application (minor), or both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal Logic's role is to ensure consistency, not to establish truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal Logic deals with equivalence of expression, conversion, opposition, syllogism, and related formal relations; its end is not truth but the Logic of Consistency — keeping inferences consistent with general formulæ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use formal logical tools to check that conclusions follow consistently from premises and that expressions are equivalent when claimed; do not treat formal equivalence as sufficient for empirical truth. Formal logic is an auxiliary to the broader logic concerned with ascertaining truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trains of reasoning arise when minors are not directly observable
rubrics_metrics.description: Trains of reasoning (chains of syllogisms) are necessary where the minor premise or the mark relied upon is not directly observable and must itself be established by other inductive arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a minor depends on inference, trace back the chain of inductions that justify it. Verify each intermediate induction and the convergence of separate inductions that bring the case within the relevant generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marks and marks-of-marks criterion for applying inductions
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine whether a new case falls under a general induction, we identify distinguishing marks (evidence) once for all; sometimes we must recognize the marks by other marks (marks of marks), possibly via several intermediate inductions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly list the marks that define applicability of an induction. If the primary marks are not directly observable, identify and validate secondary marks that serve as proxies. In complex reasoning, document the chain by which a case is brought within an induction's scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex deductions require verifying each contributing induction
rubrics_metrics.description: In complicated branches of knowledge deductions often consist of several chains (a mark of d, b of e, c of f, d e f of n) united; the ultimate inference rests on multiple inductions that must each be correct for the final conclusion to hold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For multi-chain deductions, evaluate each chain's induction independently and then assess their combination. Example: physical deductions often require verifying multiple independent marks (shape, incidence, parallelism) before concluding about focus of reflected rays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retrospective testing of reasoning is separate and advisable
rubrics_metrics.description: We often review our syllogistic and inductive processes to recognize that they have been correctly performed; this verification (collating copy with original) is good practice but is not part of the initial act of induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include an explicit verification step when possible to guard against omission of checks that casual reasoning may skip. However, do not mistake the act of testing for the inferential step itself when analyzing the psychological process.

rubrics_metrics.name: General conclusions are convenient but not necessary for particular validity
rubrics_metrics.description: If evidence is sufficient for a particular inference, it is sufficient for a corresponding general conclusion; nevertheless, forming the general proposition is a convenience and security for future inference, not a prerequisite for the particular inference's validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing a specific inference, focus on whether the particular case is warranted by evidence; treat generalization as a useful but distinct act that aids subsequent reasoning and bookkeeping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonical formulæ for equality and inequality in geometric reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: To infer equality we have formulæ such as: things which applied to each other coincide are equals; things equal to the same thing are equals; a whole and the sum of its parts are equals; sums of equal things are equals; differences of equal things are equals. For inequality analogous formulæ are listed (whole and its parts are unequals; sums/differences involving unequal things yield unequals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When attempting to prove geometric facts (e.g., base angles of an isosceles triangle), map the problem to these canonical marks of equality/inequality. If the object does not obviously exhibit those marks, construct chains of reasoning to bring the case within one of the known formulæ.
